title: Mastery Challenge: Everyday Technology
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Everyday Technology Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: electricity and power, AI and chatbots, VR, gene editing, fusion, quantum computers and how to judge new technology. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Everyday Technology Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the tree, from Level 1's stone tools and the watts on your electricity bill to chatbots, fusion and quantum computers. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Everyday Technology: mastered
learned: From stone tools to the power grid
AI, chatbots, VR and drones, explained
Gene editing, fusion and quantum computing, without the hype

questions.prompt: A phone charger supplies 5 volts at 2 amperes. What is its power?

options.label: 2.5 watts
options.rationale: That divides; multiply volts by amps.

options.label: 7 watts
options.rationale: That adds them; multiply instead.

options.label: 10 watts
100 watts
options.rationale: Far too much: 5 x 2 is 10.

questions.explanation: Volts times amps equals watts: 5 x 2 = 10 watts, 10 joules every second.

questions.prompt: Why must a power-station generator be spun by steam, water, wind or gas?

options.label: Its magnets wear out unless they keep moving
options.rationale: Magnets don't need motion to stay magnetic.

options.label: Energy can't be created, so its electricity must come from the motion it's given
Spinning cools the wires
options.rationale: Spinning the rotor is what makes the current.

options.label: The grid needs it to run on DC
options.rationale: Power stations make AC.

questions.explanation: A generator turns motion into electricity; since energy is never created, every joule starts as the energy of whatever spins it.

questions.prompt: A hospital trains an AI only on patient records from one city. What does NIST's 2022 warning suggest?

options.label: It may handle patients unlike those in its data badly
It will work equally well everywhere
options.rationale: Models often can't go beyond the kind of data they learned from.

options.label: It will learn new rules from patients it never saw
options.rationale: It learns only from its training examples.

options.label: It no longer needs any examples at all
options.rationale: Machine learning depends on its examples.

questions.explanation: NIST warns that AI absorbs the biases in its training data and often cannot extrapolate beyond the kind of data it learned from.

questions.prompt: A chatbot hands you a court case to cite. Given how language models work, what should you do?

options.label: Cite it: a confident tone means it's accurate
options.rationale: Confidence and accuracy are different things.

options.label: Ask the chatbot to sound more certain
options.rationale: Tone doesn't change the facts.

options.label: Check it in a real source, since it could be invented
Trust it only if the answer is long
options.rationale: Length says nothing about truth.

questions.explanation: Models predict probable text and can hallucinate; in 2023, lawyers were fined for citing six cases a chatbot invented.

questions.prompt: Which of these is augmented reality rather than virtual reality?

options.label: A headset that replaces your view with a wire-frame room
options.rationale: That's virtual reality.

options.label: A game world you can only see inside a sealed headset
options.rationale: Replacing the view is VR.

options.label: A flight simulator with no view of the real room
options.rationale: That's a fully artificial scene.

options.label: A yellow first-down line added to a football broadcast

questions.explanation: AR overlays computer-made images on the real scene, like the first-down line on football broadcasts.

questions.prompt: Which gene edit could be passed on to a person's future children?

options.label: Editing a patient's blood stem cells, as Casgevy does
options.rationale: Body-cell edits stay with that patient.

options.label: Editing an embryo, as He Jiankui did in 2018
Editing a bacterium's DNA in a lab dish
options.rationale: That doesn't change any person's heredity.

options.label: Editing any cell with a guide RNA
options.rationale: Only eggs, sperm and embryos pass edits on.

questions.explanation: Edits to eggs, sperm or embryos could pass to future generations; Casgevy edits body cells only.

questions.prompt: Which statement about NIF's December 2022 fusion shot is accurate?

options.label: Fusion released more energy than the lasers delivered to the target
The facility produced more energy than it drew from the grid
options.rationale: The lasers drew about 300 MJ; fusion released 3.15 MJ.

options.label: It used fission to split uranium
options.rationale: It fused hydrogen isotopes.

options.label: It released about 300 MJ of fusion energy
options.rationale: It released 3.15 MJ; 300 MJ is roughly what the lasers drew.

questions.explanation: The lasers delivered 2.05 MJ and fusion released 3.15 MJ: gain on the target, not for the whole facility.

questions.prompt: A friend says a quantum computer is just a much faster laptop. What's the best correction?

options.label: Right: it runs every program faster
options.rationale: It helps only with particular problems.

options.label: It helps with specific problems and works alongside ordinary computers
It's slower at everything, so it's useless
options.rationale: It shows promise for problems like simulating molecules.

options.label: It never makes mistakes, unlike a laptop
options.rationale: Qubits err roughly once every thousand operations.

questions.explanation: NIST expects quantum computers to help with specific problems such as simulating molecules, working together with classical computers.

questions.prompt: From Level 1's timeline to Tomorrow's Technology: which list puts these in the order they happened?

options.label: "Artificial intelligence" coined, Edison's bulb, Casgevy approved
options.rationale: Edison's bulb (1879) came first.

options.label: Casgevy approved, Edison's bulb, "artificial intelligence" coined
options.rationale: Casgevy is the most recent, from 2023.

options.label: Edison's bulb, "artificial intelligence" coined, Casgevy approved
Edison's bulb, Casgevy approved, "artificial intelligence" coined
options.rationale: The term dates from 1955, long before 2023.

questions.explanation: Edison's bulb came in 1879, McCarthy coined "artificial intelligence" in 1955, and Casgevy was approved in 2023.

questions.prompt: Level 91's spam filter is a machine-learning model. How does the EU's 2024 AI Act treat it?

options.label: It is banned, like social scoring
options.rationale: Bans cover a few practices such as social scoring.

options.label: It faces strict high-risk rules, like hiring tools
options.rationale: High-risk rules cover uses such as hiring.

options.label: It must be approved by a judge before each use
options.rationale: The Act sorts uses by risk; spam filters are minimal risk.

options.label: It is minimal-risk and faces no new obligations

questions.explanation: The AI Act matches rules to risk: spam filters count as minimal risk and face no new obligations.
